episodes.title: Dolly Parton's “9 to 5,” the true story behind the anthem (bonus)
recap: **A catchy song hiding a protest song.** "9 to 5" works as pure pop candy — you dance to it before you notice the lyrics are actually furious. That gap between the melody and the message is exactly why it became an anthem: it smuggled a real complaint about clerical work into the Top 40, and decades later people are still singing along without clocking how "messed up" the situation it describes actually is.

**The movement predates the movie.** Before Dolly, Lily Tomlin, and Jane Fonda ever got near a script, a group of Boston secretaries organized in 1973 and literally called themselves "9to5." Between the '60s and '80s there was a real sense that clerical work — overwhelmingly done by women — was on the edge of transformation, and this grassroots labor group is the actual origin of both the movie's title and its politics, not a screenwriter's invention.

**A song and a movie that still gets revisited.** This is a rerun of a 2021 episode, brought back as a bonus alongside a fresh look at how far workplace conditions for women have (or haven't) moved since. The fact that Planet Money keeps returning to it says something: the underlying tension the song describes hasn't fully resolved, which is part of why the anthem still lands.
fun_facts: The Boston secretaries who inspired the movie called their organization "9to5" — the same name the film and song later made famous.
The episode originally aired in 2021 and is being rerun as a special Sunday bonus.
Music featured includes "9 to 5," "5 to 9," and "Fly on the Wall."
discussion_questions: What made a song about frustrating, undervalued clerical work catchy enough to become a singalong anthem instead of a protest dirge?
Since the "9to5" secretaries organized in 1973, what clerical/admin-style jobs today face a similar mismatch between how essential the work is and how little cultural or economic credit it gets?

highlights.text: The Boston secretaries who inspired 9 to 5 the movie and song literally called their 1973 labor organization '9to5.'
9 to 5's brilliance is a catchy melody masking a protest message — listeners dance along before registering how bleak the lyrics are, which is part of why it became a lasting anthem.

episodes.title: Terry Fox: Greatest Canadian Hero
recap: **A kid who was never the most talented, just the most relentless.** Terry Fox wasn't a natural athlete — he was one of the shortest kids in his eighth-grade class and played a single minute of basketball all season. He just showed up early and left late until, by twelfth grade, he was co-athlete of the year at his high school. That stubborn, unglamorous persistence is the throughline for everything that came after: bone cancer, an amputated leg, and a cross-Canada run all get met with the same "just keep showing up" approach.

**Losing a leg didn't stop him — it just changed the sport.** After his right leg was amputated six inches above the knee for osteogenic sarcoma at 18, Fox didn't pause his athletic career, he redirected it: within a year he joined a wheelchair basketball team and led it to back-to-back national tournaments, training by pushing himself up mountain passes in his wheelchair instead of on flat ground. The prosthetic leg he'd later run on was primitive by today's standards — nine pounds, no shock absorption, repaired mid-run with literal car parts — which forced him into an awkward hop-skip gait that bled at the socket almost every day of the run.

**The Marathon of Hope started as a whisper and became a movement.** Fox kept his plan private at first, training quietly with his girlfriend and best friend before quietly approaching the Canadian Cancer Society, who basically shrugged him off until he lined up his own corporate sponsors — Ford donated a camper van, Adidas gave him 24 pairs of shoes, an airline flew the team to the starting line in Newfoundland. Only after he'd built that support on his own did the Cancer Society fully back him for a run of roughly 7,400 kilometers, coast to coast.

**Publicity was inconsistent, and it nearly broke the whole thing.** Local volunteers and press coverage had to precede him for donations to materialize, and it didn't always happen — in his first month he raised only $25,000, and in Quebec he got no press, no donations, and drivers who tried to run him off the road. A Toronto Star reporter, Leslie Scriver, changed everything by writing a running weekly column on him, and by the time he reached Toronto he was greeted like a national hero, meeting Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau and hockey legend Bobby Orr.

**The run ended not because he gave up, but because the cancer came back.** At roughly 3,300 miles in, a persistent cough and chest pain sent him to a hospital in Thunder Bay, where doctors found the cancer had metastasized to his lungs — a golf-ball-sized tumor in one, a fist-sized tumor in the other. He'd already passed the halfway point and hugged the entire Canada–US border by then; 143 days in, averaging 23.3 miles a day, he had to stop having already raised $2 million, double his original goal.

**He kept raising money even after he couldn't run.** A five-hour telethon in September 1980 featuring Elton John, John Denver, Gordon Lightfoot, and Anne Murray raised another $10 million, and a follow-up "dollar for every Canadian" goal brought in $24.17 million Canadian — about $93 million in today's dollars. He died of pneumonia-triggered complications on June 28, 1981, at 22, having already become the youngest person ever inducted as a Companion of the Order of Canada while still alive.
fun_facts: His prosthetic leg was repaired mid-run using parts from a '78 Malibu, and later by a welder in Sault Ste. Marie.
Three iterations of his artificial leg are on display at the Royal British Columbia Museum.
His mother, Betty Fox, was one of eight flag bearers at the 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympics opening ceremony.
The Terry Fox Foundation has raised over $1 billion for cancer research as of this year, with Terry Fox Runs held on every continent except Antarctica.
discussion_questions: Fox deliberately avoided thinking about the full 7,400-km distance and instead broke the run into single miles or even single telephone poles — what does that mental strategy suggest about how people can sustain effort on goals that otherwise feel impossibly large?

Local press coverage made or broke his fundraising town by town, decades before social media existed — how might a Marathon of Hope play out differently (better or worse) if it happened today with instant, viral distribution instead of a beat reporter following along?

highlights.text: Terry Fox broke his 7,400km run into single miles or even single telephone poles to make an impossible goal mentally survivable.
His prosthetic leg was repaired mid-run using car parts from a '78 Malibu and later by a welder in Sault Ste. Marie.
A single Toronto Star reporter's running weekly column turned Fox from an unknown runner into a national hero almost overnight, showing how earned local press can outperform any paid campaign.
The Terry Fox Foundation has raised over $1 billion for cancer research to date.
Fox kept training and running despite a doctor privately diagnosing an enlarged heart and warning him to stop if dizzy or short of breath — he simply didn't disclose it and pushed on.

episodes.title: How China Won the Car Industry
recap: **China went from "pitiful" to biggest car exporter on Earth in one generation.** When Michael Dunne first arrived in China in 1990, the only car he rode in was a Shanghai 760 — literally a copy of a 1955 German car, reserved for senior party officials. Five years ago China exported about 1 million cars; this year it's on pace for 12 million, more than the US and Japan combined, while also selling roughly 25 million domestically. China now accounts for close to 40% of global car production.

**The joint-venture strategy was the opening move, and it worked almost too well for foreigners.** Deng Xiaoping's pragmatic bet — "I don't care if the cat is black or white" — let Western automakers into China but only via joint ventures where China kept 50%+ ownership. Volkswagen, GM, and others made huge profits (GM China's president reportedly said "we're making more money than God"), but Chinese leadership grew frustrated watching foreign brands dominate their own market while China imported $100 billion a year in oil — a vulnerability with deep historical resonance in Chinese strategic thinking.

**A secret 2000 white paper planted the seed for the EV pivot.** Wan Gang, an engineer who'd worked at Audi in Germany, quietly told China's State Council the country would never catch up to the West on internal combustion engines and should leapfrog to electric instead. The idea sat dormant for a decade — early EV subsidy spending nearly matched oil-import spending with little consumer uptake — until Xi Jinping backed it hard under the "Made in China 2025" program starting around 2011.

**Tesla was the trojan horse that made the EV bet actually work.** China rolled out the red carpet for Tesla in 2019 with 100% foreign ownership (no joint venture required) specifically to import manufacturing know-how — and it worked almost too well: one supply-chain executive told Dunne that once Tesla's suppliers were local, everything Tesla knew leaked to Chinese competitors "overnight." Tesla's cultural effect — proving EVs could be desirable, not just compliant — did in China exactly what it had done in the US.

**The 2023 Shanghai Auto Show was the visible tipping point.** Dunne's friend, a former Mercedes-Benz China managing director, called it "a total shock" — for the first time, Chinese brands like Xiaomi (whose $32,000 EV rivals a Porsche/Model 3 hybrid, and which Ford CEO Jim Farley personally drives) took center stage while Western legacy brands got shunted to side halls. A BYD executive told Dunne plainly: "this is not the company you've known for twenty years."
fun_facts: The Shanghai 760 sedan Dunne rode in during 1990 was a copy of a Russian car that was itself a copy of a 1955 German design.
BYD's high-end sub-brand, Yangwang ("Look Up"), makes a car that can rotate 360° in place and drive briefly on water.
Xiaomi — a phone maker — entered the car business only five years ago and now makes a $32,000 EV comparable to a Porsche/Model 3 hybrid.
China's auto exports this year (12 million) exceed total US car manufacturing output (about 10 million).
discussion_questions: China deliberately let Tesla in with full ownership specifically to accelerate technology leakage to domestic competitors — is that a repeatable playbook for other industries, or was EVs a unique case?

Dunne notes the US has "essentially banned Chinese cars" — given how far ahead Chinese EVs reportedly are on cost and features, what's the actual tradeoff the US is making by protecting its auto industry this way?

highlights.text: China let Tesla open a wholly-owned factory (skipping the usual forced joint venture) specifically to import manufacturing know-how, and it worked so well that competitor knowledge reportedly leaked to Chinese suppliers 'overnight.'
China's car exports this year (12 million) exceed total US car manufacturing output (~10 million).
BYD's Yangwang sub-brand makes a car that can rotate 360° in place and drive briefly on water, illustrating how far Chinese EV feature engineering has advanced beyond cost competition alone.

A secret 2000 white paper by engineer Wan Gang proposing China leapfrog straight to EVs sat dormant for a decade until Xi Jinping backed it hard starting around 2011 — a reminder that big strategic bets often incubate quietly long before they're acted on.

Xiaomi, a phone maker, entered the car business only five years ago and now sells a $32,000 EV that rivals a Porsche/Model 3 hybrid — showing how fast adjacent-industry entrants can catch up once battery/software tech commoditizes hardware advantages.

episodes.title: How to balance a two-sided marketplace
recap: **A marketplace CEO who became his own customer.** Brad Wilson took the Care.com CEO role in January 2023 while his wife was dying — meaning he was simultaneously trying to fix the company's caregiver-matching problem and living the exact crisis Care.com exists to solve, as a newly single parent of three. That's not just a poignant detail; it's the reason the rest of the conversation carries real conviction instead of generic marketplace-strategy talk.

**The two-sided tension is brutally literal: keep families' costs down while paying caregivers fairly, with no easy lever to pull.** When Wilson arrived, conversion (the share of people who actually pay after posting) was under 2%, versus a typical marketplace benchmark of 2-6%. Families spend roughly 20% of income on childcare and up to 40% with senior care layered in, while caregivers aren't overpaid either — Wilson says solving this fully "without some support" from government or (mostly) employers isn't realistic.

**The unlock was stacking care needs instead of treating them as separate jobs.** Most families juggle four care categories — child, senior, pet, home — and Wilson's insight was that caregivers would rather bundle tasks in one household than commute between several partial gigs. That's a way to raise effective caregiver pay without raising the price families pay, just by cutting the caregiver's "calendar Tetris."

**Two years of infrastructure work had to happen before any of the fun stuff could ship.** Wilson describes inheriting badly outdated, federated back-end systems (authentication, messaging, payments, trust & safety) that made everything slow. He deliberately spent 18-24 months rebuilding that foundation before the team could do "fast-twitch retailing" — a classic case of needing to slow down to eventually go fast, which frustrated engineers who wanted to build visible features the whole time.

**An FTC settlement taught him to pick fights selectively.** The FTC's "dark patterns" investigation flagged Care.com's subscription cancellation flow (which Wilson agreed needed fixing) alongside claims he disputed. Rather than fight everything, Wilson settled and redirected the energy toward the product, a pragmatic call he says he made against his own instincts because advisors convinced him it was right.
fun_facts: Care.com has about 700 corporate relationships and monetizes three ways: backup care days, a care concierge staffed by master's-level social workers, and discounted digital memberships for smaller employers.
70 million people in the US have pets — Wilson's go-to stat for why caregivers can profitably take on multiple household tasks at once.
Wilson previously helped launch the Disney Bundle (helping make Disney+ the fastest-growing streaming service) and ran GM roles at HBO Max and Travelocity.
New Mexico currently has universal childcare — one of the few state-level models Wilson points to as worth watching.
discussion_questions: Wilson argues the caregiver-pay/family-affordability tension can't be solved by the marketplace alone and needs government or employer subsidy — does that make two-sided marketplaces in essential-but-underpaid labor categories structurally different from something like Uber or Airbnb?
He deliberately paused feature development for nearly two years to rebuild infrastructure — what signals should a leader look for to know that kind of pause is worth the frustration it causes?

highlights.text: Care.com's core two-sided tension — keep costs low for families while paying caregivers fairly — has no clean lever; CEO Brad Wilson argues it can't be solved by the marketplace alone without employer or government subsidy.

Wilson boosted effective caregiver pay without raising family costs by encouraging caregivers to bundle multiple household tasks (childcare, pet care, housekeeping) in one home instead of commuting between partial gigs.
Wilson deliberately spent 18-24 months rebuilding Care.com's outdated back-end infrastructure before shipping new features, despite team frustration — a case of slowing down in order to go fast.

When Wilson joined, Care.com's marketplace conversion rate was under 2%, well below the 2-6% typical for marketplaces — a red flag metric he used to diagnose how badly the matching product was underperforming.

episodes.title: How to find businesses with (almost) zero competition
recap: **The world is full of invisible million-dollar businesses hiding in plain sight.** Sam walks through the wild economics of lab-testing monkeys — one company, Charles River Labs, does $4 billion a year just running drug trials for 80% of biotech companies, and paid $500 million to buy a monkey-breeding operation just to control its own supply chain after COVID sent prices from $2,000 to $50,000 a monkey. The point isn't really about monkeys; it's that practically every object and process around you is somebody's obscure, wildly profitable business that nobody thinks to compete for.

**Warren Buffett's American Express bet is a masterclass in "gaps nobody notices."** A scam artist got loans against fake soybean oil inventory (filling storage tanks with seawater instead), and when the fraud collapsed, American Express — which had vouched for the inventory — ate a massive settlement. Buffett bought AmEx stock on the dip because he correctly bet that ordinary customers had no idea their credit card company was tangled up in an obscure "soybean oil checking" business.

**"The art of noticing" beats raw hustle for finding uncompeted niches.** Citing Paul Graham's essay "How to Do Great Work," the hosts describe following genuine interest all the way to the edge of an industry's frontier — that's where you find the tedious, unsexy gaps nobody has bothered to fix. A dental back-office biller who built a ~$10M/year business just automating insurance claims for dentists is the concrete example: an unglamorous, overlooked process most competitors never even see.

**Enthusiasm and childhood obsessions are underrated competitive advantages precisely because smart people are embarrassed to lean on them.** The hosts argue that being visibly enthusiastic feels "low status" to smart, jaded people, which means genuinely showing up excited is a near-free way to stand out. They tie this back to looking at what obsessed you as a kid (citing Dan Brown's childhood treasure-hunt Christmases as the root of his career writing treasure-hunt novels) as a signal for what you could sustainably get obsessed with as an adult.
fun_facts: A single lab-testing monkey now costs around $20,000, up from $2,000 before COVID supply shocks.
More than 20% of all drugs are tested on monkeys before reaching clinical trials.
Exploding Kittens co-creator Elon Lee has made roughly 7 of the top 10 best-selling board/card games sold at Target.
Jerry Seinfeld has handwritten jokes every morning for 40 years and compiled the rejects into a book called "Is This Anything?"
discussion_questions: The hosts argue "noticing" and "enthusiasm" are underrated because smart, competitive people feel embarrassed using them — what's an area of your own work where leaning into an "uncool" trait could actually reduce your competition?

If most durable niche businesses exist because nobody glamorous wants to look for them, does that mean the best businesses are inherently the ones you'd be reluctant to tell people about at a dinner party?

highlights.text: Charles River Labs does $4B/year in revenue by running lab testing as a service for 80% of biotech companies, then bought a $500M monkey-breeding operation just to control its own supply chain.
Warren Buffett's famous American Express stock bet stemmed from a soybean-oil-inventory fraud where a scammer filled storage tanks with seawater to fake collateral for loans.
A dental back-office biller built a roughly $10M/year business just by taking over insurance claim filing for dentists, a tedious process most competitors overlook entirely.

Citing Paul Graham's 'How to Do Great Work,' the hosts argue following genuine interest to the frontier of an industry is where you find overlooked gaps, because interest is both more motivating and more differentiating than chasing obvious opportunities.
The hosts argue enthusiasm is a near-free competitive advantage because smart, jaded people feel embarrassed being visibly enthusiastic, leaving the trait underused.

Dan Brown's father gave him treasure maps instead of presents every Christmas, planting the obsession that later became the treasure-hunt structure of The Da Vinci Code — a case for mining childhood interests for career direction.
